pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 11–13 (KS3) — contrast photosynthesis (energy from sunlight) with chemosynthesis (energy from oxidising chemicals like hydrogen sulphide); hydrothermal-vent communities where chemoautotrophic bacteria are the producers supporting tube worms, giant clams and vent crabs with NO sunlight; what this implies for the origin of life; why NASA studies vents as analogues for possible life on Europa and Enceladus.
• Standards — UK (DfE KS3): biology 'photosynthesis as the key process for food production' and cellular respiration/energy — chemosynthesis as an alternative producer pathway; nutrition and food webs.
• Standards — US (NGSS): MS-LS1-6 (role of photosynthesis in cycling matter/energy) and MS-LS2-3 (energy flow through an ecosystem) — extended to a non-photosynthetic base.
• Operational details: the core is the PRODUCER-ENERGY-SOURCE contrast — both photosynthesis and chemosynthesis fix carbon into food, but one is powered by light and the other by chemical energy (oxidising H2S from vent fluid). Bacteria are the base of a vent food web independent of the Sun. The big-idea tail is genuinely open/speculative: vents as a candidate cradle for life's origin, and as Earth analogues guiding the search for life on icy ocean moons — questions science is still debating.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~11, concrete): states vent bacteria make food from chemicals, not light; Tier B (transitional): contrasts photosynthesis and chemosynthesis by energy source and builds a vent food web with bacteria as producers; Tier C (formal, ~13): explains why vents inform origin-of-life and astrobiology (chemical energy + water ± sunlight), evaluating the reasoning behind Europa/Enceladus missions.
bestPractices: Teach chemosynthesis by direct contrast with the already-known photosynthesis: same job (producers making food/fixing carbon), different energy source (chemical vs light) — an analogy that scaffolds the new idea.
Make bacteria the visible PRODUCERS at the base of the vent food web, correcting the assumption that producers must be green/plants.
Use a real vent community (chemoautotrophic bacteria → tube worms/clams → crabs) so energy flow from a chemical source is concrete.
Frame the origin-of-life and astrobiology material as OPEN questions with evidence and reasoning to weigh, not settled facts — model scientific argumentation.
Connect explicitly to the 9–11 deep-sea topic ('life without sunlight') and to KS3 photosynthesis to bind the sequence together.
keyRepresentations: A side-by-side photosynthesis vs chemosynthesis comparison (inputs, energy source, product)
A vent food-web diagram with chemoautotrophic bacteria as producers
A vent cross-section: mineral-rich fluid → bacteria → tube worms/clams/crabs
An astrobiology analogue panel: Earth vent ↔ Europa/Enceladus subsurface ocean
commonMisconceptions: 'All producers photosynthesise / all food chains start with sunlight' — the key misconception chemosynthesis overturns.
'The vent's HEAT is the energy source for the food web' — conflating heat with the chemical energy bacteria actually oxidise.
'Producers must be plants/green' — not recognising bacteria as producers.
'Chemosynthesis is just photosynthesis in the dark' — missing that the energy source is fundamentally chemical, not light.
Treating origin-of-life/alien-ocean claims as proven rather than as reasoned, evidence-based hypotheses.

learn.summary: Ages 11–13 (KS3; NGSS MS-LS1-6, MS-LS2-3): teach chemosynthesis by direct contrast with the already-known photosynthesis — both are producers fixing carbon from CO2 into food, but one is powered by light and the other by chemical energy (oxidising hydrogen sulphide, H2S, from vent fluid). Build a hydrothermal-vent food web where chemoautotrophic bacteria are the producers at the base, supporting tube worms, giant clams and vent crabs with no sunlight as the energy source. Then weigh the open, still-debated questions: could life have begun at vents, and why do agencies like NASA study vents as analogues for possible life on icy ocean worlds such as Europa and Enceladus? Key targets include correcting 'all producers are green plants / all food chains start with sunlight', distinguishing chemical energy from the vent's heat, and distinguishing an energy source from a food source.

activities.title: Build a vent food web on a different power source
feedback: If a learner keeps the Sun at the base: no sunlight reaches a deep vent — point to exactly where sunlight enters the ENERGY path. If you can't, the producers' energy must be something else. (Some marine snow does drift down, and the oxygen in seawater comes from photosynthesis at the surface, but the vent's PRODUCERS build food using chemical energy, not light.)

If a learner picks the vent's heat as the food energy: heat is not what the bacteria capture to build food. They oxidise a chemical (H2S) and use that chemical energy — line up heat vs chemical energy explicitly.

If a learner says bacteria 'eat' or 'feed on' H2S: just as plants don't eat sunlight, vent bacteria don't eat H2S — they use its chemical energy to synthesise their own food from CO2. Keep CO2 as the carbon source.

If a learner calls it 'photosynthesis in the dark': both processes build food (sugar) from CO2, but the energy input differs — light for photosynthesis, chemical for chemosynthesis. Same kind of food made, fundamentally different fuel (and different by-products: photosynthesis releases oxygen, while H2S oxidation produces sulfur or sulfate).
activities.rationale: Assembling and running two contrasting webs is intended to make the producer-energy contrast and the energy flow explicit and manipulable, rather than asserted. Choosing a base that fails (sunlight in the dark) and one that works (chemical energy) targets the misconception that all food chains start with sunlight. A side-by-side comparison panel scaffolds the new idea onto the known photosynthesis case. Linked sunlit/vent builders, a selectable base energy source, and a vent cross-section showing fluid feeding the bacteria are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory.
sourceClaims: Chemosynthesis lets bacteria at hydrothermal vents produce food using chemical energy (e.g. oxidising hydrogen sulphide) instead of sunlight, forming the base of a vent food web that supports tube worms, clams and crabs with no sunlight.
learnerActions: First build (or label) a familiar sunlit web: Sun → phytoplankton/plants → consumers, and mark where the energy enters.
Now build a hydrothermal-vent food web set in permanent darkness. Try to place the Sun at the base and notice it cannot power this web — no sunlight reaches kilometres down.

Choose the base's actual energy source from options including 'sunlight', 'the vent's heat', and 'chemical energy (oxidising hydrogen sulphide, H2S)'. Select the chemical-energy option so chemoautotrophic bacteria become the producers.
Extend the web: bacteria → tube worms / giant clams → vent crabs, and trace the energy flow from the chemical source upward.
Set the two webs side by side and fill a comparison table: inputs, energy source, and product (food/organic matter from CO2) for photosynthesis vs chemosynthesis.
activities.intendedInsight: Photosynthesis is not the only way to build a food web. Producers do the same job — making food by fixing carbon from CO2 — but can be powered either by light (photosynthesis) or by chemical energy from oxidising H2S (chemosynthesis). Bacteria, not green plants, are the producers at a vent, and the community's energy source is chemical, not the Sun.

activities.title: Reason with an astrobiologist: did life begin at vents, and where else might it be?
feedback: If a learner treats origin-of-life or alien-life claims as proven: these are reasoned, evidence-based hypotheses still being debated — distinguish what is observed from what is inferred.

If a learner dismisses the moons because 'there's no sunlight': that's the point — vent communities show sunlight isn't required as the energy source, so the relevant question is whether chemical energy, water and minerals are present.
Push for the mechanism of the analogy: name what Earth vents and the moons' suspected environments have in common (chemical energy + water ± minerals) rather than just asserting they are similar.
activities.rationale: The open tail of this topic is genuine unsettled scientific argument, well suited to in-role dialogue where a learner may probe reasoning and weigh evidence and uncertainty. This is intended to model scientific argumentation and frame speculative material honestly as hypotheses. Dialogue is a companion to the mechanism work, not a replacement for building the food web.
sourceClaims: Hydrothermal vents are studied as analogues for possible habitats on icy ocean worlds (Europa, Enceladus) and are relevant to hypotheses about the origin of life, because they combine chemical energy, water and minerals.
learnerActions: Take on the question in role: ask and answer 'Why look at hydrothermal vents to search for life beyond Earth?' and 'Could life have begun at vents?'

Set out the reasoning: if life needs chemical energy, water and minerals — which vents supply without sunlight as the energy source — then sunless environments elsewhere are not automatically lifeless.
Apply the analogy to Europa and Enceladus: these icy moons may have subsurface oceans and hydrothermal chemistry but no sunlight; discuss what makes them candidates and what remains unknown.
State explicitly which parts are established (vent communities exist and run without sunlight as their energy source) and which are open hypotheses (origin of life at vents; life on ocean moons).
Weigh at least one piece of evidence for and one source of uncertainty before giving a tentative, reasoned position.
activities.intendedInsight: Vents reshape the search for life because they show a food web can run on chemical energy and water rather than light. Whether life began at vents, and whether ocean moons host life, are genuine open scientific questions to be argued from evidence and uncertainty — not settled facts.

activities.title: Explore and interrogate a vent cross-section
feedback: Producer check: the producers here are bacteria, not plants and not animals — producers need not be green.
Energy vs carbon check: the energy source is chemical (H2S oxidation); the carbon source is CO2. Keep these distinct.
If a learner expects a sunlight input in the energy path: there is none — trace the arrows and confirm the base's energy is chemical, not light.
activities.rationale: A clear tappable exposition presents the vent anatomy, the two-process comparison and the astrobiology analogue cheaply and accessibly. It does not itself let a learner build and run the alternative-energy web, so it works best as support alongside the builder rather than as the construction task.
sourceClaims: Chemosynthesis lets bacteria at hydrothermal vents produce food using chemical energy (e.g. oxidising hydrogen sulphide) instead of sunlight, forming the base of a vent food web that supports tube worms, clams and crabs with no sunlight.
learnerActions: Explore a labelled vent scene: mineral-rich fluid rising, bacterial mats, tube worms, giant clams and vent crabs — tracing which organism depends on which.
Open a photosynthesis/chemosynthesis comparison showing inputs, energy source and product aligned for each.
Examine an Earth-vent ↔ Europa/Enceladus analogue panel and state what the two settings share.
Answer short checks: name the producer at a vent; name its energy source (oxidising H2S) and its carbon source (CO2); and explain why the community survives with no sunlight as its energy source.
activities.intendedInsight: A vent community is a complete food web whose base producers are bacteria powered by chemical energy, with no sunlight as the energy source; the same comparison that defines photosynthesis clarifies how chemosynthesis differs.

activities.title: Check and discriminate the concept
feedback: Gap response (insists the base energy traces to the Sun; claims sunlight seeps down or that drifting detritus feeds the WHOLE community): re-establish chemosynthesis as a genuinely independent energy pathway — the producers' energy is from vent chemicals, not light.

Partial response (says 'chemosynthesis' but can't name H2S oxidation as the energy source or keep CO2 as the carbon source): press for the mechanism — what is oxidised for energy, and where does the carbon come from?
Full response: bacteria oxidise H2S for energy to build food from CO2, cleanly contrasted with photosynthesis, placed at the base of the web, and transferred to astrobiology reasoning.
Asking 'how do the bacteria capture it?' forces the mechanism rather than just the label — require the energy step, not a one-word answer.
activities.rationale: A two-tier diagnostic that asks both the judgement (is the Sun the source?) and the mechanism (how is energy captured?) is designed to discriminate a learner who over-generalises photosynthesis from one who holds the concept. Recognition and short-answer items check the contrast but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction the builder provides.
sourceClaims: Chemosynthesis lets bacteria at hydrothermal vents produce food using chemical energy (e.g. oxidising hydrogen sulphide) instead of sunlight, forming the base of a vent food web that supports tube worms, clams and crabs with no sunlight.
learnerActions: Answer a two-tier diagnostic: given giant tube worms and clams thriving around bacteria in permanent darkness, decide whether sunlight is the energy source the producers capture — and if not, state what is and how the bacteria capture it.

Give the full answer: chemoautotrophic bacteria oxidise H2S (using oxygen dissolved in seawater) for energy and use it to build food from CO2; tube worms, clams and crabs depend on those bacteria; the energy the producers capture is chemical energy from vent fluid (from reactions in the Earth's crust), not sunlight.
Compare a leaf and a vent bacterium: what is the same (both build food from CO2) and what differs (light energy vs chemical energy)?
Predict: if a vent stopped emitting hydrogen sulphide, what happens to the tube worms, and why?
Contrast the two energy sources, identify the vent producer, and reason about how far the Europa/Enceladus analogue holds and what remains unknown.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure understanding means naming chemosynthesis, identifying the oxidised chemical (H2S) as the energy source, keeping CO2 as the carbon source, and transferring the idea to origin-of-life and ocean-world reasoning — not merely using the word 'chemosynthesis' as a label.

constraints: Scaffold onto prior knowledge: introduce chemosynthesis as a contrast with the already-taught photosynthesis, and connect to the earlier deep-sea 'life without sunlight' topic.
Keep energy source distinct from carbon source throughout: bacteria oxidise H2S for ENERGY and fix CO2 as their CARBON; never let learners conclude bacteria 'eat' H2S.
Keep chemical energy distinct from the vent's heat; heat is not the food energy the bacteria capture.
Producers need not be green or plants — bacteria are the producers at a vent; address this explicitly.
Frame origin-of-life and Europa/Enceladus material as open, evidence-based hypotheses under active debate, never as settled fact.
State the vent's sunlight-independence as being about the ENERGY SOURCE (chemical, not light); do not overclaim that no surface-derived material of any kind reaches the deep sea.

Tappable/exposition and recognition items check and present the concept but do not themselves elicit independent construction of the alternative-energy food web; use them alongside the builder rather than as the only task.
A 3D vent dive can add atmosphere but the conceptual payload (energy-source contrast, food web, astrobiology reasoning) is not spatial; do not treat immersion as required for the learning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; both sources carry verified:false and have not been re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Both cited sources (NOAA Ocean Exploration; NASA Ocean Worlds) are listed as verified:false in the source row; treat the science claims as plausible but unconfirmed in this rewrite.
The origin-of-life and ocean-moon (Europa/Enceladus) material is inherently speculative in the source and should be taught as open argument; do not present it as established.
The source's astrobiologist-dialogue and food-web-builder descriptions are proposed designs; retained as options with their stated affordances and limits, not as evidence of efficacy.

Scientific nuance held outside learner text: the vent community is independent of sunlight for its ENERGY SOURCE (correct, and the taught objective), but aerobic vent chemosynthesis commonly uses dissolved oxygen ultimately generated by surface photosynthesis. Beyond KS3 scope; learner-facing statements are scoped to the energy source to stay accurate without overclaiming total sunlight-independence.

Also beyond scope but noted for accuracy: some drifting detritus (marine snow) does reach deep water, so the correction to learners targets 'the base/whole community traces to the Sun', not the stronger false claim that nothing from the surface ever arrives.

probeDeeper: You said energy traces to the Sun. A vent has run in total darkness for thousands of years — point to exactly where the Sun enters that food web. If you can't, what does that imply?
What's the same, and what's different, between a leaf and a vent bacterium in how each gets its energy and its carbon?
Why would NASA send missions to icy moons with no sunlight but suspected hot vents on the seabed — what are vents telling them?
If a vent stopped emitting hydrogen sulphide tomorrow, what would happen to the tube worms, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: No — vent communities are independent of sunlight. Their base is CHEMOSYNTHESIS, not photosynthesis: chemoautotrophic bacteria get energy by oxidising chemicals (especially hydrogen sulphide, H2S) streaming from the vent, and use that energy to build food (organic matter) from CO2. Tube worms, clams and vent crabs then depend on those bacteria. So the ultimate energy source is chemical energy from the Earth's interior, not the Sun. This is why vents matter for ideas about the origin of life and why agencies like NASA study them as analogues for possible life on ocean worlds such as Europa and Enceladus, where there is no sunlight but there may be hydrothermal chemistry.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'All food energy on Earth ultimately comes from the Sun' — treats photosynthesis as the only possible base of any food web.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish chemosynthesis as a genuinely independent pathway: the energy comes from vent chemicals, not light. Contrast the two energy sources side by side.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Sun — all food energy starts with photosynthesis, so it must reach the vent somehow.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists the Sun must be involved somewhere; claims sunlight seeps down or that detritus from above feeds the whole vent community.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Chemosynthesis and photosynthesis are basically the same, just in the dark' — blurs the energy source.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line them up: both build food from CO2, but photosynthesis uses LIGHT energy while chemosynthesis uses CHEMICAL energy (oxidising H2S). Same product, different energy input.
errorPatterns.distractor: They're the same process — the bacteria just do photosynthesis in the dark.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes bacteria 'photosynthesising without light', or can't say what differs between the two processes.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The bacteria eat the chemicals like food' — confuses an energy source with a food source.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Clarify producer logic: like plants don't 'eat' sunlight, vent bacteria don't 'eat' H2S — they use its chemical energy to synthesise their own food from CO2.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the bacteria 'feed on' hydrogen sulphide as if it were a meal, not that they use it to MAKE food from CO2.

responseLevels.gap: Insists all energy traces to the Sun; cannot name a non-light energy source or conflates the two processes.
responseLevels.full: Explains chemosynthesis mechanistically (bacteria oxidise H2S for energy to build food from CO2), contrasts it cleanly with photosynthesis, places it at the base of the vent web, and transfers the idea to origin-of-life / ocean-world astrobiology reasoning.
responseLevels.partial: Knows vent life doesn't use sunlight and can say 'chemosynthesis', but treats it as a label — can't identify H2S oxidation as the energy source or keep CO2 as the carbon source.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: At a hydrothermal vent, kilometres down in permanent darkness, giant tube worms and clams flourish around bacteria — with no sunlight ever reaching them. A student says 'the energy must still trace back to the Sun somehow, because photosynthesis is where all food energy on Earth begins'. Is the Sun the ultimate energy source for a vent community? If not, what is, and how do the bacteria capture it?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student who over-generalises photosynthesis insists the energy must trace to the Sun and cannot name the chemical source; a student with the concept names chemosynthesis, identifies the oxidised chemical (H2S) as the energy source, and keeps CO2 as the carbon source. Asking 'how do the bacteria capture it' forces the mechanism, not just the label.
